Illegal character '{0}'.

Invalid number format: '{0}'.
column6: A number is decimal digits without a leading zero, or '0x', '0b' or '0o' followed by digits of that base: octal 63 is '0o77', not '077'; '09' and '077' are not number tokens. In an entry argument and a conversion text a leading zero is decimal ('077' is 77).

This string literal is not closed.
column6: A string ends with the quote character it starts with ({0}). Add the closing quote; to put a quote character inside the string, write it with a backslash.

Unterminated comment: {0}.
column6: Close the comment with '*/'.

column6: Check and correct the escape sequence.

Syntax error: {0}.
Expected '{0}' before {2}, to close the '{1}'.
column6: Every '{1}' needs its '{0}'. The note shows the '{1}' that is still open here.

Unexpected '{0}': no '{1}' is open here.
column6: Remove the '{0}', or add the '{1}' it was meant to close.

column6: A conditional is written: if <condition> then <value> else <value>. Each branch may be a block: if c then {{ ... }} else {{ ... }}.

Unexpected ';': there is no statement between it and the ';' before it.
column6: Statements are separated by a line break or by one ';'. Remove the extra ';'.

'=' assigns; it cannot be used in the condition of an 'if'.
column6: To compare, write '==': if x == 1 then ...

'{0}' is a keyword and cannot be used as a name.
column6: Choose another name, for example '{0}_'.

Expected {1} before {0}.
column6: The items of a list (parameters, arguments, elements) are separated by ','.

The declaration of '{0}' has no value.
column6: A declaration binds a name to a value: let {0} = <value>, or with a type: let {0}: <type> = <value>.

Expected {0} before {1}.
Unexpected {0}{1}.

column6: Something opened earlier is not finished: check the last declaration of the file.

column6: A '<' directly after a name, a literal or a closing bracket starts '<...>' arguments, as in f<a>(x). If a comparison is meant, put a space before the '<': a < b.

This '>' follows a space and is read as the comparison operator, so the angle-bracket list it was meant to close is still open at {0}.
column6: The '>' that closes '<...>' touches the last item or starts its line: f<a, b>. Directly inside '<...>', a '>' after a space is a comparison (xs->filter<(x: int) => x > 1>).

A statement cannot start with '{0}': the line break before it ended the statement of the line above.
column6: A line break ends a statement unless the line is visibly unfinished. To continue an expression on the next line, end the line with the operator ('a +', then 'b'). An operator that can only be binary ('*', '->', '&&', '==', ...) also continues the expression when it starts the next line.

An interpolation has no expression to format.
column6: Write an expression between '${{' and '}}': ${{value}}. For a literal '${{' write '\${{'.

This '>' is read as a comparison with the next line, which starts with {0}: two statements may have been joined into one.
column6: A '>' after a space, at the end of a line, is the comparison operator, and the expression goes on with the next line. The '>' that closes '<...>' arguments touches the last argument; a chain of comparisons (a < b > c) is never what a program means.

An error has occurred: {0}.
Redeclaration of reference: '{0}'.
column6: Each identifier must be declared only once in its scope.

Module '{0}' not found. {1}
column6: Check if the module path is correct or add the directory to search paths.

Identifiers starting and ending with double underscores are reserved for internal use.
column6: Avoid using names like '__example__'; choose different identifiers. To overload an operator, write 'func operator +(a: V, b: V): V'.

Tuple unpacking requires the same number of references and data nodes, or exactly one tuple data.
column6: Ensure the number of variables matches the number of unpacked data elements, or use a single tuple value.

Invalid {0} literal: '{1}'.
column6: Ensure the literal '{1}' is valid and supported by the language.

Duplicate key in dict: '{0}'.
column6: Make sure all keys in a dictionary are unique.

Parameter reference must be unqualified: '{0}'.
column6: Use the parameter name without namespace or scope qualifiers.

Data for parameter '{0}' must be static.
column6: Ensure the parameter data is a compile-time constant or literal.

Duplicate parameter detected: '{0}'.
column6: Remove or rename the duplicated parameter.

Unresolved type reference: '{0}'.
column6: Ensure the type is defined and visible in the current scope.

Unresolved reference: '{0}'.
column6: Make sure the name is declared and in scope.

Return type mismatch between branches (in function '{0}'): expected '{1}', found '{2}'.
column6: Ensure all branches of if-else or match-case expressions return the same type.

Invalid access index: '{0}'.
column6: Ensure the index is within bounds for arrays or refers to a valid field in structs.

Type '{0}' does not support index access.
column6: Check the type and ensure it is a tuple or a struct that supports indexing.

No matching function found for argument types: {0}.
column6: Check the number and types of arguments to ensure they match one of the available overloaded function signatures. Available overloads: {1}

Function of type '{0}' cannot be called with argument types: {1}.
column6: Check that the function type '{0}' matches the number and types of arguments provided ({1}).

Return type '{0}' does not match the function's declared return type '{1}'.
column6: Ensure that the value returned from the function matches the type specified in the function signature: {2}. No implicit conversion is applied: convert explicitly, for example float(x) for a number or 'x as T' for a module type.

Cannot insert data of type '{1}' into a(n) {0} with element type '{2}'.
column6: Ensure the data type matches the {0}'s element type, or convert the data to the appropriate type before inserting.

Cannot call function '{0}' with type '{1}' as its type is not fully constructed yet.
column6: This often occurs when a function without an explicit return type calls itself, preventing the compiler from inferring the actual return type. Consider explicitly specifying the function's return type to avoid this issue.

column6: A literal the type cannot hold is not wrapped around or cut off, and a value is never cut to fit a type. Write a value the type holds, or give the literal a wider type.

Dynamic cast from '{0}' to '{1}' is not allowed.
column6: Use types that allow safe conversion, or ensure the conversion is valid. Nothing is converted implicitly: a text becomes a number with 'int(s)' or 'parse_int(s)' ('float(s)', 'parse_float(s)' for a float), a number of another type with 'float(n)', and a module type with 'v as T'.

Failed to parse module file: {0}.
column6: Check the file for syntax errors.

Invalid operator URI format: '{0}'. Expected 'protocol:path'.
column6: Use a valid operator URI in the form protocol:path (e.g. std:add).

Executor protocol '{0}' not found.
column6: Check that the protocol is registered or refer to the documentation for supported operator protocols.

Entry module '{0}' must define a resolvable 'main' on the module root (__root__).
column6: Add a top-level main function or ensure it is registered as a direct root subgraph.

Invalid call to '{0}' with argument types {1}: {2}.
column6: The argument kinds match the operator's signature, but their statically known properties (such as tensor shapes or dtypes) are incompatible. Fix the arguments or relax their static types.

'{0}' is immutable and cannot be passed to a var parameter of '{1}'.
column6: Only a variable declared with 'var' (or a var parameter) can be modified. Declare it with 'var', or bind the new value to a new name.

The target of an assignment must be a variable, or a path from one.
column6: A path is a variable followed by any number of fields and elements: 'var p = {{ x: 1 }}; p.x = 2' and 'var xs = [1, 2]; xs[0] = 2' are assignments of the whole variable (design principles 3.5). Any other expression is a temporary, and a store into it would go nowhere: assign the value to the whole variable instead.

'{0}' is not supported: {1}.
column6: The grammar accepts this construct, but the compiler does not implement it. Remove it; nothing in the language replaces it yet.

The arguments of the type '{0}<...>' are not accepted: {1}.
column6: What a type takes between '<' and '>' is defined by the type itself (a type argument, or a constant written 'const <data>'). An argument a type does not accept is an error; it is never ignored.

The call to '{0}' needs an explicit conversion: {1}.
column6: A type that leaves open what a parameter fixes is never accepted implicitly, and nothing is checked on its behalf. {2} A conversion written with 'as' is checked when it runs; a value that does not fit stops the program at that position.

The returned value needs an explicit conversion to the function's declared return type '{0}': {1}.
column6: A type that leaves open what the declared return type fixes is never accepted implicitly, and nothing is checked on its behalf (function signature: {3}). Where the value is known to fit, write the conversion: {2}. A conversion written with 'as' is checked when it runs; a value that does not fit stops the program at that position.

internal: # 0x000025 was ImportCycle: modules may import each other (design principles 10.1).
# 0x000026 was ImportedFunctionUsesModuleValue: a function of another module may use the
# top level of its own module since every module builds into one root graph.

The name '{0}' is imported from the modules '{1}' and '{2}' with {3}.
column6: Two imports that bring the same name with the same parameter types conflict, and so do two that bring a value of the same name; neither is chosen silently. Give one of them another name where it is imported ('import {{ name as other_name }} from m'), or import the name from one of the modules only and reach the other through its module ('import m', then 'm::name').

internal: # An error: the construct it reports is not compiled, so a program that uses it must not
# run. It used to be a warning (0x100000), and the declaration that used the feature was
# dropped while the rest of the program went on.

The feature '{0}' is not supported yet.
column6: Check the documentation for supported features.

internal: # Generic functions and type functions (design principles 5.6).

The type parameter '{0}' is declared twice at the head of this declaration.
column6: A declaration declares each type parameter once, after its name: 'func first::<T>(xs: T[]): T'. A call names them by position or by name ('f::<T = int>').

The type variable '{0}' of '{1}' can never be bound: {2}.
column6: A type variable must remain present in a parameter or result type. Its position must be reachable through arrays, tuples, structs and function types.

The generic function '{0}' cannot be called with argument types {1}: {2}.
column6: A type variable takes the type of the argument found at its first binding position, or, when that argument says nothing (a 'null', a generic function that is itself waiting for its types), at another occurrence; every parameter is then checked against its type with the variables replaced. Result-only variables take their types from the expected result or explicit f::<T> arguments. A value enters a 'T?' or 'T!' parameter by itself; nothing else is converted. Signature: {3}

The generic function '{0}' cannot be given its types here: {1}.
column6: A generic function may stand wherever a function is expected, also as an argument of another generic function. It is a template: the compiler builds the instance once the position fixes its type variables (a parameter of function type, a declared type, the other arguments of the call). Here they are not fixed. Signature: {2}

Instantiating the generic function '{0}' with {1} is refused: {2}.
column6: Each call of a generic function with a new set of types builds a new subgraph. A generic function that calls itself with ever larger types never stops doing so.

The type function '{0}' cannot be used this way: {1}.
column6: A type declared with parameters, e.g. 'type Pair<T> = (T, T)', is used with one type argument per parameter between '<' and '>', e.g. 'Pair<int>'.

The generic function '{0}' cannot be {1}.
column6: This use of a generic function is not supported.

'{0}' is used as a value here, but it names {1}, not one function.
column6: Only a name that stands for exactly one function has a function value. Wrap the call in a function whose parameter types are written out, e.g. '(x: int) => {0}(x)'.

'throw' needs a function declared to return 'T!': {0}.
column6: 'throw e' returns an error value, as 'return' returns a value, so the function it stands in must declare a fallible return type, for example 'func f(): int! {{ ... }}'. It does not unwind to a caller.

'throw' takes an error value, not a value of type '{0}'.
column6: Make one with 'error(kind, message)', for example 'throw error("ParseError", "not a number")', or hand on the one a 'case error e' bound.

The type '{0}' marks '{1}' twice.
column6: 'T?' may be null and 'T!' may have failed; a second mark of the same kind adds nothing a program could tell apart. 'T?!' and 'T!?' are allowed.

A value of type '{0}' cannot be used here: {1}.
column6: A value that may be null ('T?') or may have failed ('T!') is opened only by '??', '!!', '?->' and by 'match' with 'case null' / 'case error e'.

'try'/'catch' is not part of Camel.
column6: An operation that can fail returns a value of type 'T!'. Give a fallback with 'a !! b', hand an error on with 'x ?-> f', or inspect it with 'match r {{ case error e => ... case v => ... }}'. Faults (division by zero, an index out of range) are not errors and end the program; isolating them is the job of the fault-isolation operator.

'{0}' cannot be applied here: {1}.
column6: 'a ?? b' needs 'a' of type 'T?' and 'b' of type 'T' (the result is a 'T') or 'T?' (the result is a 'T?', so that 'a ?? b ?? c' tries each in turn). 'a !! b' needs 'a' of type 'T!' and 'b' of type 'T' or 'T!'. 'x ?-> f' needs 'x' of type 'T!' and a function 'f' that takes a 'T'.

This 'match' on a value of type '{0}' is not well formed: {1}.
column6: A 'match' on a 'T?' has exactly the cases 'case null' and one other ('case v' binds the value, 'case _' ignores it). A 'match' on a 'T!' has exactly 'case error e' and one other.

internal: # Reporting several errors (0x80 and up, clear of the blocks above).

Cannot import module '{0}': it has errors ({1}).
column6: The errors are reported for that module. This one follows from them and goes away when they are fixed.

The type '{0}' cannot be a key of '{1}': {2}.
column6: A key of a Map and an element of a Set must have an order and an equality that cannot change: 'int', 'i32', 'bool', 'string', tuples of those, and an enum every field of which is one of those. The value type of a Map is not restricted.

The key '{0}' is written twice in this literal converted to '{1}'.
column6: A map holds one value per key. In an array computed when the program runs the later entry replaces the earlier one; in a literal a repeated key is taken for a mistake. Remove one of the two entries.

internal: # Rulings of 2026-10-12 (design principles log 2.10): 0xB0 and up.

This 'match' on a value of type '{0}' has no 'case _'.
column6: A 'match' must have a default case: add 'case _ => ...' for the values the cases do not list. A 'match' on a bool that has both 'case true' and 'case false' is complete, and so is one over 'T?' or 'T!' with its two fixed patterns.

This 'if' has no 'else' and is used as a value.
column6: An 'if' without 'else' has no value: its arm may be of any type and what the arm gives is dropped. It can only stand as a statement. Where a value is wanted, add an 'else' arm of the same type ('if c then 1 else 0'), or make the result nullable ('if c then 1 else null').

'{0}' is bound to an empty array '[]' that has no element type.
column6: The empty array literal takes its element type from where it stands: a declared type, a parameter, the other arm of a branch, an 'as'. Here there is none. Write the type: 'let {0}: int[] = []'.

The context arguments <{0}> cannot be bound to '{1}' as a value: {2}.
column6: 'f<w>' used as a value is a partial application: a function that already has its context ('with') arguments, 'let g = inc<1>' then 'g(2)'. It needs 'f' to be one function that takes these arguments. Called in place, 'f<w>(x)', the arguments of the call choose the function.

The source of this list comprehension has type '{0}', which has no elements to take.
column6: A list comprehension '[e for x in xs if c]' is 'xs->filter<(x) => c>->map<(x) => e>': 'xs' must be an array (or another value 'map' and 'filter' accept), and 'x' has the type of its elements.

internal: # Rulings of 2026-10-13 (design principles log 2.11): 0xC0 and up.

The {1} side of '{0}' has type '{2}', not 'bool'.
column6: '&&' and '||' are branches on a 'bool': 'a && b' is 'if a then b else false', 'a || b' is 'if a then true else b'. The right side is evaluated only when the left side does not decide, both sides are 'bool', and neither operator can be overloaded. For logic that evaluates both sides (element-wise logic on tensors, an operator of a type of your own) use '&' and '|'.

internal: # Modules and namespaces (design principles 10.1, 10.2): 0xD0 and up.

The variable '{0}' cannot be exported.
column6: A 'var' of the top level of a module is read and written only by the module's own functions: export the functions that read and write it ('export sync func bump(): int sync {{ wait cnt += 1; return cnt }}'). A 'let' can be exported.

The value '{0}' depends on itself: {1}.
column6: The values of the top level of modules are computed before 'main' starts, each from the values it uses: directly, through the functions its initializer calls, and through the values those use, in any module. A value cannot be computed from itself. Compute one of the values in the chain without the other, or turn it into a function.

The function '{1}' uses '{0}' only after it is called in its own recursion, where the call could not pass it.
column6: A function that calls itself, directly or through other functions, must use a variable it captures, or be complete, before the recursive call that would pass it: a call is ordered among the uses of the variables it was known to use, and a function value holds what the function captured when it was made. Use '{0}' before the recursive call, or pass it as a parameter.

The name '{0}' is ambiguous here: {1}.
column6: Two 'using namespace' in force bring something of this name that cannot be told apart: a value or a type from each, or functions of the same parameter types. Write the qualified name of the one meant.

internal: # (AnyBranchSubject) and 0xE2 (AnyNotAllowed) are retired: there is no `any` type, and
# writing it is an ordinary unknown name. Their codes are not reused.
# The condition and the cases of a branch (found with the `any` cases above).

The condition of this 'if' has type '{0}'; a condition is a 'bool'.
column6: There is no truth-value conversion: compare explicitly ('n != 0', 'len(s) > 0', 'x != null').

This case of a 'match' on a value of type '{0}' is a value of type '{1}'.
column6: A case is compared with the value matched, so the type of that value must accept it. Write the case as a value of that type, or convert the value matched first.

internal: # Rulings of 2026-10-14 (design principles log 2.12) on operators and on collections that
# are not changed in place: 0xF0 and up.

The result of '{0}' is not used, and '{0}' changes nothing: it returns a new value{1}.
column6: The operations of the standard library return new values and leave their arguments as they were: after 'let ys = xs->append<5>', 'xs' is unchanged. To change a variable, bind it to the result, 'xs = xs->append<5>', as 'x = x + 1' does for a number.

'{0}' cannot be overloaded: {1}.
column6: The operators that can be overloaded are the binary '+', '-', '*', '/', '%', '^', '@', '==', '<', '<=', '>', '>=', '&', '|', indexing '[]', and the unary '-', '!', '~'; '!=' follows '=='. '&&', '||', '??', '!!', '->', '?->', '..', 'as', assignment and compound assignment are constructs of the language.

This overload of operator '{0}' is not valid: {1}.
column6: A binary operator takes two parameters and a unary one takes one ('-' may take one or two); indexing takes the indexed value and at least one index. An operator has no with-parameters and no var parameters.

Operator '{0}' is already defined for ({1}){2}.
column6: The overloads of an operator from every module, the built-in ones included, are one set: each must take parameter types that no other one takes.

internal: # A call (of a function, an operator or a partial application used as a value) that
# more than one overload takes: several candidates in the pass being used, never
# settled by declaration order (design principles 5.1). Renamed from
# AmbiguousOperatorCall when it became the report for every call; the code is unchanged.

The call to '{0}' with ({1}) fits more than one overload.
column6: More than one function takes these arguments; make the choice explicit: annotate the literal with its type (for example '2 as f32') or convert an argument with 'as'. The overloads that take them: {2}

internal: # Rulings of 2026-10-15 (design principles log 2.13) and the defects found with them: 0x110

This value has type '{0}', which is not the declared type '{1}'.
column6: A declaration written with a type takes a value of that type; nothing is converted on the way (a number does not become a float by itself, and a text does not become a number). Convert the value explicitly: 'float(n)' for a number of another type, 'int(s)' or 'parse_int(s)' for a text, 'string(n)' for a number written as text (the same for 'i32', 'f32', 'f64' and the complex types), 'v as T' for a module type; or change the declared type.

The type '{0}' is part of a cycle of types: {1}.
column6: Each of these types needs the next one to be declared first, and the last needs the first: none of them can be. Remove one of the references that close the cycle. A type may contain itself only through an array, a map, a set or an enum (design principles 5.2).

The annotation '@{0}' is not accepted: {1}.
column6: A line that starts with '@' annotates the function declaration or the block that follows. '@name' and '@name<args>' are decorators of a function or of a block; '@name(args)' is no longer accepted (numeric permissions are tags, design principles 7.2). A tag is written with '#': '#name', '#name<args>' or '#[a, b<v>]' (design principles 6.2).

internal: # The structured loop (design principles 3.10): 0x120 and up.

'for' takes the elements of an array, a string, a map or a tensor; '{0}' has type '{1}'.
column6: A loop's 'for x in xs' visits the elements of xs in order (design principles 3.10): the elements of an array; the code points of a string, each a one-character string; the (key, value) pairs of a map, in key order (11.3); and the sub-tensors of a tensor along its first dimension. 'range(a, b)' is the array of the integers from a to b.

The body of this loop gives a value of type '{0}'; the state of the loop has type '{1}'.
column6: The initial state fixes the state type. Return that type after 'do', or change the initial value (for example, '0.0' instead of '0' for a float state). With multiple state names, return a tuple in the same order.

The first value of the loop state '{0}' does not give it a type ('{1}').
column6: The state of a loop has the type of its first value. 'null' and the empty array '[]' have none of their own: write 'null as T?', or bind the empty array with its type first ('let none: int[] = []') and start from that name.

The condition after 'while' has type '{0}'; a condition is a 'bool'.
column6: There is no truth-value conversion: compare explicitly ('n != 0', 'len(s) > 0', 'x != null').

The name '{0}' is declared twice in this loop head.
column6: The names of a loop's state and the name 'for' binds to the element are declared together, for the condition and the body; each is given once.

internal: # Rulings of 2026-10-19 (design principles log 2.13): the nominal enum, 0x130 and up.

The variant '{0}' is declared twice in enum '{1}'.
column6: A variant is one of the values of its enum and is written by its name; each name occurs once.

The field '{0}' is declared twice in variant '{1}' of enum '{2}'.
column6: A field of a struct variant is written by its name; each name occurs once.

The variant '{0}' of enum '{1}' carries {2} field(s): write '{3}' to build one.
column6: A variant without a field list is a single value; one with fields is built by writing the fields after its name, 'Shape::Circle(1.0)' or 'Shape::Rect {{ w: 1.0, h: 2.0 }}'.

The variant '{0}' of enum '{1}' takes {2} field(s), but {3} were given.
column6: The fields of a variant are those its declaration writes: as many, and in the same order for a variant written with '(...)'.

The pattern '{0}' does not match a value of type '{1}': {2}.
column6: A pattern names a variant of the enum it matches and, if that variant has fields, binds each of them by its position ('Shape::Circle(r)') or by the name its declaration gives ('Shape::Rect {{ w, h }}').

The match over '{0}' has no case for {1}, and no 'case _'.
column6: Every variant of an enum is a value of it, so a match that names variants must name all of them or end with 'case _'. The compiler adds no arm the program does not show.

'{0}' is a value of enum '{1}': its fields are not read by name or index.
column6: A field of a variant is taken out by matching the value and binding it in the arm of that variant: 'match v {{ case {2} => ... }}'.

internal: # 0x137 and 0x138 reported the retired forms `A | B` and `T ? U`; the parser no longer reads
# either, so they are gone and their codes are not reused.

Cannot infer the type argument '{0}' of enum '{1}' from the fields of '{2}'.
column6: The fields of the variant do not say what the argument is; where the value is used the expected type does: 'let x: Option<int> = Option::None'.

Field {0} of variant '{1}' has type '{2}', but the value given has type '{3}'.
column6: The fields of a variant are those its declaration writes.

Variant '{0}' of enum '{1}' cannot be built from this value: {2}.
column6: A variant written with '(...)' is built from its fields in order; one written with '{{ }}' from a value that has a field of each name it declares; and one without fields is the value itself.

internal: # Named dimensions of type extents (design principles 5.4): 0x140 and up.

The dimension name '{0}' is bound here, but only a parameter type can bind one.
column6: A dimension name binds where it first appears in a parameter type, 'x: Tensor<f32, [n, 3]>'. Every later occurrence, including one in the return type, writes 'n'.

The dimension name '{0}' is not bound by any parameter of this signature.
column6: A name in a type's extents is bound by its first plain occurrence in a parameter type, 'x: f32[n]', and later occurrences write it. A name that appears only in the return type is an error: the caller has no argument that could say what it is.

The dimension name '{0}' is already bound; write '{0}' here.
column6: Only the first occurrence of a dimension name in the parameter types binds it; later occurrences write it. Dimension names and pack names are separate namespaces, so one name cannot be both.

Argument {0} has extent {1}, but the dimensions the earlier arguments bound do not allow it.
column6: The dimensions a signature names are one value for the whole call: every argument whose type writes the same name must have the extent the name was bound to.

This is not a shape: the extents of a type written with dimension names are integers, bound names, or linear expressions over them ('f32[n, 3]').
column6: Each extent is a non-negative integer, a dimension name bound by the signature, or a linear expression over such names: 'n', 'n + 1', '2 * n', 'n - k'. A dimension that is not linear is unknown, and an unknown extent is written '?'.

The function cannot be differentiated: {0}.
column6: grad and with_grad differentiate the first `with` parameter of a function that returns a float (design principles 9.9). The generic function '{0}' is instantiated with {1} while that same instance is being built, and its return type is not known yet.

The type '{0}' has no fields for a 'static for' to walk.

The key '{0}' of a 't.[...]' access is not known when the function is compiled.

The block for the field '{0}' of '{1}' gives no value, so the comprehension has no element for it.

internal: # Body-less declarations, the declarations of a C++ module's operators (design principles

The declaration '{0}' names the operator '{1}', which no loaded module implements.

The declaration '{0}' names the operator '{1}', which another module declares.
column6: A module declares only the operators it implements: a body-less declaration stands for an operator of the module it is written in, and declares no other module's operator. Write the declaration beside the implementation, or call the operator through the module that declares it.

The type of the parameter '{0}' of this lambda is not written and cannot be inferred: {1}.

internal: # `typeof` and the same-shape comprehension (design principles 5.6, generic-structure
#/ The expression after `typeof` has no value, so the type it stands for cannot be taken.

typeof {0} has no value type: {1}.
column6: `typeof` takes the type of a value. Write an expression that produces one, or name the type directly.

typeof is written inside the larger type {0}.
column6: `typeof` stands for a whole type. Bind the value in a `let` and name its type, or write the enclosing type out.

column6: A same-shape comprehension names a struct or a tuple type; a leaf has no fields.

The shape {0} is filled from the fields of {1}.

internal: # Type identity in `match type` (`case int`, `case T`; design principles 5.5). 0x1C2.
#/ An identity pattern names a type that cannot select the subject: `void`, a `typeof`
#/ expression, an open type variable, a type written twice in one case, or a type that an

The identity pattern '{0}' cannot select a type here: {1}.

internal: # Folding a call of a pure function with constant arguments (handover H271). 0x1C5 and up.
#/ An argument of a call in a place that needs a constant is not one.

The call of '{0}' cannot be evaluated at build time: {1}.
column6: A call in a place that needs a compile-time constant is evaluated only when every argument is a constant itself: a literal, the 'n' of a 'static for', a 'constas' value, or an expression the compiler can evaluate. Make the argument a constant, or move the call to a place where a runtime value is accepted.

The call of '{0}' cannot be evaluated at build time: {1}.
column6: Only a pure call is evaluated: a function with no effects and no reads of mutable state. Remove the effect from the declaration, or call it where a runtime value is accepted.

internal: #/ The call nests deeper than the evaluator follows: it recurses without a base case here.

The call of '{0}' cannot be evaluated at build time: {1}.

The call of '{0}' cannot be used as a compile-time constant: {1}.
column6: A compile-time value is a number, a bool, a string or a character. Return one of those from the function, or move the call to a place where a runtime value is accepted.

internal: #/ The call's body uses a construct this build-time evaluation does not read.

The call of '{0}' cannot be evaluated at build time: {1}.

# 4.4, handover H276). 0x1CD and up, after the constant-folding codes of h271. The `with`

column6: A default is evaluated where the declaration is, not at each call, so it can only be a constant expression.

internal: #/ The default of an ordinary parameter has a type that does not fit the parameter.

The argument '{0}' of '{1}' has type '{2}', not '{3}'.

Variable parameters are only allowed in sync functions.

{0} is neither waited nor in a sync block, and {1}.

column6: A tag only allows a pass to do something; with no such pass in the pipeline the tag has no effect. Add the pass it names ('read_by'), or remove the tag.

internal: # A dimension name is written once in a signature, so it relates nothing (design principles
# 5.4): write `?` if the size is not meant as a relation.

The dimension name '{0}' is written once in this signature, so it relates nothing.

internal: # Type variables (design principles 5.5). A head name written nowhere is a warning: the
# declaration is still well formed, it just declares a parameter nothing can fill.
#/ A type parameter is declared at the head of a declaration and written nowhere in its

column6: A type parameter is one the declaration uses in a parameter or result type; a declaration that writes it nowhere can never take a type for it. Write it in a type, or remove it from '::<...>'.

column6: A translation pass only translates the graph the preceding passes left. Run the passes named in the message before it, or remove the construct it cannot express.

column6: The pass gave up without a diagnostic of its own: it built or was given a graph it cannot handle, which is a defect of the compiler rather than of the program. Try the pipeline without this pass or with the passes in another order, and report the program together with the pass list.

'{0}' could not be evaluated by std::macro: {1}.
column6: Every argument of this macro call is a constant, so std::macro evaluates it ahead of time. A failed evaluation is a fault during the run of the pass, not a compile error: the program stops before it runs, and the output the evaluation produced before the failure stays. Without std::macro in the pipeline the call runs with the program.

No value was given for the {0} {1} of 'main'.
column6: The parameters of 'main' are the inputs of the program. To run it, give each one a value on the command line: --arg name=value (a number; a complex number written as the language writes one, such as 1+2i or 0.5-0.25i, or a real number such as 1.5 for its real part; true/false or text for a scalar; a .npy file for a tensor; a directory of .npy files for a struct of tensors). No default is assumed.

Cannot bind the argument '{0}' of 'main': {1}.
column6: An argument is written --arg name=value, where name is a parameter of 'main' and value is read according to the parameter's declared type.

Cannot write the result of 'main' to '{0}': {1}.
column6: --output <file> (-o) writes the value 'main' returns: a number, bool or text as a text file, a tensor as a .npy file, a struct or tuple as a directory with one file per member. Without it the value is printed on standard output.

Out of memory{0}: {1}.
column6: The graph, permanent and meta spaces hold the compiled program (its runtime graphs, its types, the constants of the graphs being compiled) and grow with it; each has a total limit that only guards against a compiler that does not stop allocating. If the program is this large, raise the limit with the environment variable the message names. If a pass is named, the growth may be its doing (an inlining or unrolling that does not end): run the pipeline without it. The auto space holds run-time values: it is bounded by the memory of the host, or by CAMEL_GC_HEAP_LIMIT_MB when that is set, in which case the values the program keeps alive do not fit the limit.

Check the path and the permissions of the directories on it.

column6: The `#gpu` tag promises that the device runs everything written in the scope, including the functions it calls; an operator the device back end cannot build a program for is a compile-time error there, never a host execution. Change the operator, its shape or the function it is written in, put it under `#cpu` where the scope allows that, or remove the tag; `--devices cpu` runs the whole program on the host.
